# Reduce image noise

- Route: `/tools/reduce-image-noise`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `reduce-image-noise`

## Summary

Separate luminance and color noise reduction with a live preview, then export at full resolution. (Photo editing)

## Details

Noise reduction in Aperture is a Detail layer with two sliders, Luminance and Color, each 0 to 100. Both run in the Lab color space: luminance noise is smoothed with an edge-aware bilateral filter on the L channel, while color blotches are smoothed with a plain Gaussian blur on the a and b channels, which is why you can be far more aggressive on Color than on Luminance before anything looks soft. The layer sits in the same non-destructive stack as every other adjustment, so you can mask it to the shadows with a luminosity range, lower its opacity, or drop it later. The preview updates as you drag; the exported file is rendered from the original pixels with the same arithmetic. Use the Judge at 100% button before you decide, because noise is invisible at fit-to-screen zoom.
### What it does
- Smooths luminance noise with a 9 by 9 bilateral filter on the Lab lightness channel, so edges above the range threshold are preserved while flat areas average out.
- Smooths color noise with a separable Gaussian on the Lab a and b channels, removing the purple and green speckle that high ISO leaves in shadows.
- Keeps the two kinds of noise independent: Color at 60 with Luminance at 0 cleans chroma blotches and leaves every bit of grain-like texture intact.
- Lives on an adjustment layer with opacity, blend mode and an optional mask, so you can denoise only the sky or only the shadows.
- Renders the export from the original file on our server with the same formulas, at full resolution rather than from the screen preview.
### How to use it
1. Drop in the photo: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF or BMP. The Detail panel opens in front with Noise reduction visible.
2. Zoom to 100%: Press Judge at 100% so each image pixel is one screen pixel. At fit-to-window the noise is averaged away and every setting looks fine.
3. Set Color, then Luminance: Raise Color until the colored speckle disappears, usually 40 to 70. Then raise Luminance only as far as the grain bothers you; 20 to 40 keeps texture.
4. Export: Pick JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF and a quality. The server denoises the original and encodes the file; the original is never modified.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- HEIC, HEIF, TIFF and BMP need an account so the server can make a decodable preview copy; the other formats open directly in the browser.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### Technical details
- Luminance: the image is converted to CIE Lab (D65) and L is scaled to 0..1. A bilateral filter with a fixed 9 by 9 window (radius 4 pixels, edge pixels replicated) is applied with spatial sigma 2 + 6 l and range sigma max(0.2 l, 0.001), where l is the Luminance slider divided by 100. At Luminance 50 that is a spatial sigma of 5 px and a range sigma of 0.1, which is 10 Lab lightness units; at 100 the spatial sigma is 8 px and the range sigma 0.2.
- Color: the Lab a and b channels are blurred with a separable Gaussian whose sigma is 6 c pixels, c being the Color slider divided by 100, so Color 50 is a 3 px sigma and Color 100 a 6 px sigma. Taps run from minus ceil(3 sigma) to plus ceil(3 sigma), normalized in float64, with edge pixels replicated.
- The filtered L, a and b are converted back to sRGB with the standard inverse matrix and the result is clamped to 0..1. Because the window and sigmas are in pixels, the same slider value smooths a larger share of a 1920 px preview than of a 6000 px original; judge the result at 100% zoom and expect the export to look slightly less smoothed than the fit-to-screen preview.
- A Luminance of 0 skips the bilateral pass entirely and a Color of 0 skips the Gaussian, so a layer with both at 0 is a true identity, not a very weak blur.
- The preview is drawn on your GPU in WebGL2 from a 1920 px copy of the photo, the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a documented tolerance: noise reduction carries the loosest tolerance in the Aperture parity policy, a mean error of at most 3 8-bit levels and a maximum of 12, while color adjustments are held to a mean of 1 and grain is bit-exact.
### When not to use it
Do not use noise reduction on a photo that is actually sharp but was saved at a very low JPG quality: blocky 8 by 8 compression artifacts are not noise and the bilateral filter preserves their edges rather than removing them. Re-encode from the original if you have it. If the problem is motion blur or missed focus, no amount of smoothing helps either; try the Sharpen page for small softness. For a deliberately grainy film look you want to add grain, not remove it, and the Grain sliders in the same Detail panel do that with a bit-exact export.
### Use cases
- Concert and night shots at ISO 6400: Color 60 removes the magenta and green blotches in the blacks; Luminance 30 calms the grain without erasing stage haze.
- Shadow recovery after a big Exposure push: Lifting shadows by 2 EV amplifies noise that was hiding. Add noise reduction above the exposure layer and mask it to a luminosity range of the darks.
- Old scanned prints: Scanner noise is fine and mostly luminance. Luminance 40 with a light Color pass of 20, a 1.2 px Gaussian, is usually enough; keep Texture at 0 afterwards.
- Product photos on a dark backdrop: Denoise only the backdrop with a color range mask on the background, so the product edges keep every pixel of detail.
### FAQ
Q: Why does the photo look clean in the preview but still a little noisy after export?
A: The filter window is measured in pixels. On the 1920 px preview a 9 by 9 window covers a bigger fraction of the frame than it does on the full-size original, so the export smooths relatively less. Judge at 100% zoom, which shows the real pixel scale.
Q: What is the difference between the Luminance and Color sliders?
A: Luminance runs a bilateral filter on the Lab lightness channel and preserves edges; Color runs a Gaussian on the Lab a and b channels and only affects hue and saturation speckle. Color can usually go much higher than Luminance.
Q: Is this AI denoising?
A: No. It is a deterministic bilateral and Gaussian filter pair that costs nothing per use and runs in the preview instantly. The only steps in the editor that use an AI model are Select subject and Heal.
Q: Can I denoise only the shadows?
A: Yes. Give the noise reduction layer a Luminosity range mask, set From brightness 0 and To brightness around 0.35 with a feather, and the midtones and highlights keep their full detail.
Q: Does noise reduction change the colors?
A: The Lab round trip is exact to well under one 8-bit level on flat areas. Strong Color values can desaturate tiny colored details such as distant fairy lights, because they are averaged with their surroundings.
Q: Should I sharpen before or after denoising?
A: Put the sharpen layer above the noise reduction layer so the unsharp mask sees the smoothed image; sharpening first would amplify the grain the denoise then has to remove.
